rollups.text: Probability topics Craig studied: basic favorable-outcomes/total-outcomes calculations with coins and dice (2024-01-10); addition rule, mutually exclusive and independent events, and event notation (2024-01-10); permutations and combinations (2024-01-10, 2024-04-05); card draws and conditional probability without replacement (2024-01-10, 2024-02-15, 2024-04-05); Bayes’ theorem (2024-02-15); binomial probabilities and quality-control applications (2024-01-10, 2024-04-05); tree and Venn diagrams (2024-02-15, 2024-04-05); complement rule and birthday paradox (2024-04-05).

Craig’s recurring learning preferences: gentle, clear, beginner-friendly, step-by-step explanations with concrete examples and calculations (2024-01-10, 2024-02-15, 2024-04-05); checking his solutions and comparing alternative methods (2024-02-15, 2024-04-05); starting with coin-toss examples (2024-01-10, 2024-02-15); visual aids, especially tree diagrams for dependent events (2024-02-15, 2024-04-05); combining algebraic formulas with diagrams for complex problems (2024-04-05). He found the complement method clearer and more practical for the birthday paradox than direct counting (2024-04-05).

Craig’s probability learning: On 2024-01-10, the 44-year-old Port Michael colour technologist began learning probability from scratch, aiming to apply it to paint-batch quality control. He studied basic coin/dice probabilities, event rules, counting, and card examples, and requested beginner-friendly step-by-step help. On 2024-02-15, he practiced conditional probability and dependent card draws, tree diagrams, Bayes’ theorem, and combinations; he reported 88% on a 12-question dependent-events quiz. On 2024-04-05, he advanced to permutations and combinations, the birthday paradox, complement rule, Venn diagrams, and binomial quality-control models; he reported 95% on a final assessment and an average puzzle-solving time of 10 minutes. Elapsed time from start to latest dated development: 86 days.

Craig’s goal to solve 10 probability problems involving single events with at least 80% accuracy was first stated for completion by 2024-02-01 (2024-01-10). At that point, he reported five coin-toss problems completed and 4/5 correct, but other statements that day conflicted about whether he had done any coin-toss problems, so exact progress was uncertain. He later stated the same 10-problem, 80%-accuracy goal with a 2025-02-01 deadline (2024-04-05); no completion result is recorded. The stated deadline shifted by one year and elapsed time between the two goal records was 86 days.

Craig’s colour-technology quality-control application began with paint batches: on 2024-01-10 he explored multinomial probabilities for target proportions of 20% blue, 30% red, and 50% green, and sampling batches with chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, control limits, and corrective actions. On 2024-04-05 he explored a binomial model for defects in a 100-unit batch with a 5% defect rate and possible defect thresholds. The assistant’s reported probabilities for exactly five defects and more than ten defects were inaccurate; the actual values are approximately 18.0% and 1.15%, respectively. Elapsed time between the two dated discussions: 86 days.

Recorded probability-study performance and practice: on 2024-01-10 Craig reported 4/5 coin-toss problems correct (80%) and separately mentioned possible 90% accuracy on a quiz, without a result confirming it; he also reported three study hours, including two on coin/dice, and five completed coin-toss problems. On 2024-02-15 he reported conditional-probability accuracy rising from 60% to 85% over two weeks on eight problems, and 88% on a 12-question dependent-events quiz; he also reported four study hours, including three card-draw and five dice-roll scenarios. On 2024-04-05 he reported 90% accuracy on the last five of 12 permutation/combination problems, later a rise from 75% to 92% after practicing 15 such problems, and 95% on a final assessment. These are separate reported measures, not one continuous standardized score.

Craig reported changes in problem-solving time: over six weeks, average time for complex probability puzzles fell from 20 minutes to 12 minutes, an 8-minute (40%) reduction (2024-04-05); he later said his average problem-solving time was 10 minutes (2024-04-05). The dates of the two April reports do not establish the precise elapsed time between them.

Craig reported study-session durations of three hours, including two hours on coin-toss and dice problems (2024-01-10); four hours with an extra hour of dice practice (2024-01-10 and 2024-04-05); and four hours practicing dependent-event problems, including three card-draw and five dice-roll scenarios (2024-02-15). The records may describe separate sessions and should not be summed as a single total.

rollups.text: Craig reported a permutations-and-combinations quiz score rising from 75% to 92% after 15 practice problems on 2024-04-05, a gain of 17 percentage points (about 1.13 points per problem as a simple average). He believed the improvement felt roughly linear but was told this does not establish correlation or causation.
